newsitem.title: USA: Minn. session to address education funding, wages.
newsitem.headline: Minn. session to address education funding, wages.

text.p: Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson has not decided when to open a special session to wrap up funding requests, but stadiums and ice arenas are not on the agenda, a spokesman said.
Legislative leaders "indicated no desire" to include financing a new Minnesota Twins ballpark or St. Paul arena in the special session, spokesman Brian Dietz said late Tuesday.

Carlson and lawmakers agreed to consider the governor's education funding proposal, an increase in the minimum wage and pay increases for state agency employees and legislators during an upcoming session, Dietz said.

The Minnesota Legislature late Monday approved a $22 billion biennium budget for the period beginning July 1. It included nearly $90 million of additional bond authority, a $500 million one-time property tax rebate and $234 million of longterm tax reforms.
Lawmakers included increased education funding, three more school days, statewide testing and early childhood programs, but no tax credit/deduction plan sought by Carlson.
Late Monday, Carlson announced he would veto the education package and call a special session to reconsider his plan.
The governor has proposed a $150 million credit residents could use for private school tuition, tutors, computers for school use and other education related expenses, Dietz said.
An aide said Tuesday that St. Paul Mayor Norm Coleman had hoped a special session could include financing for a new downtown arena to replace the aging St. Paul Civic Center.

St. Paul has agreed to put up $30 million for a new $130 million arena to attach to its convention center complex downtown. Private investors hoping to receive a National Hockey League franchise have offered another $35 million if they are awarded a team.
Lawmakers failed to reach an accord for $65 million of mostly bond-financed state funding before closing their session late Monday, leaving half the financing unresolved.

Erich Mische, Coleman's director of strategic planning, said that there is still time to resolve funding issues before the NHL makes its decision on expansion and St. Paul officials are exploring other private sector support for the arena.

"It's not an issue of the public saying that the ownership isn't doing its fair share," Mische said. "The real issue is trying to get through a legislative process in an environment where people are wary of professional sports issues. I think we have succeeded, in large part, in ameliorating those types of concerns."
The NHL has chosen investor groups in St. Paul, Atlanta, Columbus, Ohio, Houston, Nashville and Oklahoma City as finalists for future expansion.
The NHL expansion committee is scheduled to meet next in June.
